claims.claim: In Middle-earth one can hardly put a foot down without stirring the dust of history; the world is heavy with past.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (Time and Tide, 1954), reproduced at TheOneRing.com
claims.quote: without stirring the dust of history

claims.claim: The invented names alone are a feast.
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: The book marks the unashamed return of gorgeous, eloquent heroic romance in an anti-romantic age.
claims.quote: heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed

claims.claim: No other prose writer has captured the piercing, high, elvish beauty Tolkien achieves.
Keeping the reader aware of parallel story-lines adds immensely to pathos, irony and grandeur.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, 'The Dethronement of Power' (1955), via kate_nepveu's reading notes
claims.quote: adds immensely to the pathos, irony, and grandeur

claims.claim: The first chapter is a little shy-making, but once the story moves the initial archness disappears.
claims.source: W. H. Auden, 'The Hero Is a Hobbit' (NYT, 1954), excerpted at Epistle of Dude

claims.claim: Tolkien possesses an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.claim: By the end one knows the histories of Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves and their landscape as well as one's own childhood.
claims.quote: as well as one knows one's own childhood

claims.claim: The hobbits closely resemble the arcadian rustics of British detective fiction.
The language of portal-quest fantasy is elaborate in the anthropologist's or pre-Raphaelite painter's way, intensely descriptive and exploratory.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: the elaboration of the anthropologist or the pre-Raphaelite painter

claims.feature: reader positioned at a point of entry
claims.claim: Mendlesohn treats The Lord of the Rings as portal-quest rhetoric in which the reader learns the world from a point of entry, the process traced in her chapter one.
claims.quote: we learn from a point of entry

claims.claim: Descriptions sound vividly detailed but give an open-ended outline the reader fills in, so readers feel they helped make the world.
claims.source: Steve Walker, interview on The Power of Tolkien's Prose (Tolkien Library)

claims.claim: Scholars missed Tolkien's style because sentence-level style is not on the sociological critic's radar, though it mattered greatly to Tolkien.

Like a folk mythology the legendarium comes in many forms, with multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail (Bratman's Estate essay does not name the four modes attributed to him elsewhere).
claims.source: David Bratman, 'The History of Middle-earth' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail

claims.claim: Olsen's close reading tracks changes in tone as The Hobbit's stakes grow and distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves through their speech.
claims.source: David Oberhelman, Mythopoeic Society review of Corey Olsen, Exploring J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit
claims.quote: changes in tone as the stakes become greater

verdicts.trueWording: "you can hardly put your foot down... without stirring the dust of history"
verdicts.note: Lewis: 'in the Tolkinian world you can hardly put your foot down anywhere from Esgaroth to Forlindon... without stirring the dust of history.' The 'heavy with past' limb is carried by the next sentence: 'Our own world... hardly seems so heavy with its past' (i.e. Middle-earth is heavier). Quote exact.

Exact on the page. 'Invented' is the claim's gloss, but the surrounding sentence is explicitly about Tolkien's sub-creation of 'the whole world... theology, myths, geography, history, palaeography, languages', so the gloss is carried by context.

verdicts.trueWording: "it makes not a return but an advance or revolution"
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the book 'marks the return' of heroic romance — Lewis calls exactly that formulation 'inadequate' and says that in the history of Romance itself it is 'not a return but an advance or revolution: the conquest of new territory'
verdicts.note: Quote 'heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed' is verbatim, inside the sentence 'To say that in it heroic romance, gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed, has suddenly returned at a period almost pathological in its anti-romanticism, is inadequate.' The anti-romantic-age limb is supported; the unqualified 'return' limb is the one Lewis explicitly overrides (he concedes only that 'To us, who live in that odd period, the return and the sheer relief of it is doubtless the important thing').

verdicts.trueWording: "of which no other prose writer has captured so much"
verdicts.note: Lewis: names are best 'when they embody that piercing, high, elvish beauty of which no other prose writer has captured so much.' Quote exact. Source's comparative is 'so much' (degree) rather than an absolute none-at-all; the claim's phrasing 'the beauty Tolkien achieves' preserves that sense.

verdicts.trueWording: "adds immensely to the pathos, irony, and grandeur of the tale"
verdicts.note: Nepveu's notes on Lewis's 'The Dethronement of Power': by 'never allow[ing]' the reader to forget the connection between the parallel stories, the structure 'adds immensely to the pathos, irony, and grandeur of the tale.' Both limbs on the page; the essay is dated 1955 there, as claimed. Source is a reader's summary quoting Lewis, which the citation states.

verdicts.trueWording: "once the story gets moving, this initial archness disappears"
verdicts.note: Auden: 'I think some readers may find the opening chapter a little shy-making, [b]ut they must not let themselves be put off, for, once the story gets moving, this initial archness disappears.' Quote exact. Auden hedges the first limb as 'some readers may find'; the claim states it flatly. Page carries 'A. D. 1954', supporting the date.

verdicts.trueWording: "an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description"
verdicts.note: Auden: 'Mr. Tolkien is fortunate in possessing an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.' Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "as well as one knows one's own childhood"
verdicts.note: Auden: 'by the time one has finished his book one knows the histories of Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves and the landscape they inhabit as well as one knows one's own childhood.' Quote exact (curly apostrophe on page); 'their landscape' = 'the landscape they inhabit'.

verdicts.trueWording: "resemble very closely those arcadian rustics... British detective stories"
verdicts.note: Auden: hobbits 'in their thinking and sensibility resemble very closely those arcadian rustics who inhabit so many British detective stories.' Quote exact. The source restricts the resemblance to thinking and sensibility (explicitly contrasted with their three-foot, hairy-footed physical description); the claim drops that restriction but does not reverse it.

verdicts.trueWording: "the elaboration of the anthropologist or the pre-Raphaelite painter"
verdicts.note: Mendlesohn: 'The language of the portal fantasy is often elaborate, but it is the elaboration of the anthropologist or the pre-Raphaelite painter, intensely descriptive and exploratory rather than assumptive.' Quote exact, under her heading 'The Portal-Quest Fantasy'. Source hedges with 'often' and adds 'rather than assumptive'.

verdicts.trueWording: "In chapter one I will trace precisely this process in The Lord of the Rings"
verdicts.note: Both limbs on the page: 'portal fantasies require that we learn from a point of entry' (quote exact) and 'In chapter one I will trace precisely this process in The Lord of the Rings'; the chapter roster names 'chapter one (portal-quest fantasy)'.

verdicts.trueWording: "sounds vividly detailed... actually giving us an open-ended outline"
verdicts.note: Walker: 'tolkien's writing, too, sounds vividly detailed... but he's actually giving us an open-ended outline... that invites us to picture for ourselves'; 'lure us into filling in the blanks'; and 'The reason we feel so attached to Middle-earth, as if we've been there, is because we have been -- we help imagine it.' The quoted phrase appears as 'Its invitational quality'. All three limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "Style isn't on our scholarly radar... though that mattered a lot to Tolkien himself"
verdicts.note: Walker: 'Style isn't on our scholarly radar. Our best readers these days are mostly sociological critics... we haven't noticed much about his writing style, though that mattered a lot to Tolkien himself.' Quote exact and every limb supported; the page says 'style'/'writing style' generally, so 'sentence-level' is the claim's narrowing, neither stated nor denied there.

verdicts.trueWording: "Like a genuine folk mythology... multiple versions in differing styles and levels of detail"
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Negative limb checked and holds: the word 'mode' appears nowhere in the Estate essay, and no four-part stylistic scheme (annalistic/antique/appendical or otherwise) is named — 'annals' occurs only as the name of a text-type in the volume summaries.

verdicts.trueWording: "His discussion of the 'silly' singing elves of Rivendell highlights the differences"
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Olsen distinguishes High Elves from Mirkwood elves 'through their speech' — Oberhelman attributes the contrast to Olsen's discussion of the singing elves of Rivendell and to close readings of the songs, and never says the two kinds are told apart by speech
verdicts.note: First limb verbatim: Olsen 'traces certain themes such as Bilbo's choices, luck and providence in his adventures, and the changes in tone as the stakes become greater throughout the course of the novel.' Second limb's substance is adjacent — 'His discussion of the "silly" singing elves of Rivendell highlights the differences between these High Elves and the lower ones of Mirkwood' — but the page grounds it in song and in Olsen's discussion, not in a speech contrast between the two groups.
